title: Episode 144: Ulysses S. Grant and the First War on Terror: Crushing the Ku Klux Klan (1871)
description:
In 1871, the promise of American freedom was dying in a wave of midnight terror. Across the post-Civil War South, the Ku Klux Klan—a paramilitary terrorist insurgency led by former Confederate officers—waged a ruthless campaign of assassinations, whippings, and arson to strip four million newly enfranchised African Americans of their constitutional rights. Refusing to stand by as the fruits of Union victory were dismantled, President Ulysses S. Grant took bold, unprecedented action. Partnering with his courageous Attorney General Amos T. Akerman, Grant persuaded Congress to pass the Ku Klux Klan Act, created the Department of Justice, suspended habeas corpus, and unleashed federal troops to arrest thousands of terrorists. This is the riveting story of America's first federal war on terror—and how Ulysses S. Grant completely crushed the first Ku Klux Klan.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome back to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Today, we conclude our portrait of Ulysses S. Grant by examining the most courageous, yet frequently overlooked, chapter of his presidency: his relentless campaign to destroy the first Ku Klux Klan. Faced with a secret army of hooded terrorists that had subverted local law enforcement across the South, Grant declared a national emergency and wielded the full might of the federal government to defend the civil rights of Black citizens. Here is George with the full story.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: THE INVISIBLE EMPIRE RISES
In December 1865, in the law office of Judge Thomas Jones in the sleepy town of Pulaski, Tennessee, six bored young Confederate veterans formed a secret social fraternity. Borrowing the Greek word 'kyklos,' meaning circle, they christened their club the Ku Klux Klan. What began as a juvenile club of costumed pranksters rapidly metastasized into the most lethal and widespread domestic terrorist insurgency in American history. Within eighteen months, former Confederate cavalry general Nathan Bedford Forrest was chosen as the Klan's first 'Grand Wizard' at an organizational convention in a Nashville hotel. The Klan transformed into the violent, paramilitary arm of the defeated Southern Democratic establishment, dedicated to a single ruthless objective: the overthrow of Reconstruction and the total restoration of white supremacy.

Riding by night draped in white sheets, grotesque horned masks, and red hoods designed to resemble the ghosts of Confederate dead, Klan dens launched a campaign of calculated savagery across the South. Their targets were newly enfranchised African Americans and white Southern Republicans who dared to exercise their constitutional rights. Black political organizers were pulled from their beds and lynched in woods; schoolhouses built by the Freedmen's Bureau were torched; Black farmers who purchased land were whipped and their crops burned. In Florida alone, more than one hundred and fifty political assassinations were committed in a single county. By 1870, local law enforcement across vast swaths of Georgia, Alabama, Mississippi, and South Carolina had completely collapsed, paralyzed by fear or actively complicit in the atrocities.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: 'LET US HAVE PEACE': A GENERAL TAKES THE OATH
In 1868, Ulysses S. Grant won the presidency in a decisive electoral victory. His campaign slogan—'Let Us Have Peace'—captured the profound longing of a battle-weary nation to turn the page on a decade of bloody conflict. Grant had never sought political power; he entered the White House as a political novice, hoping to preside over a quiet, orderly reconciliation between North and South. But the reports pouring into the executive office from across the former Confederacy made it horrifyingly clear that peace was a lethal illusion. While the war of armies had ended at Appomattox, a low-intensity guerrilla insurgency had taken its place, nullifying the Thirteenth and Fourteenth Amendments at gunpoint.

Grant's moral compass was clear and unwavering. Unlike many Northern politicians who were growing exhausted by Southern troubles, Grant believed that if the federal government failed to protect the four million Black citizens who had fought for the Union and helped save the Republic, the sacrifices of the Civil War would be rendered meaningless. Speaking before Congress, Grant warned that a condition of lawlessness and organized terror existed across the southern states that local authorities were either unable or unwilling to control. The President was determined to act, but he needed a legal weapon and a fearless prosecutor to lead the assault.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: AMOS T. AKERMAN AND THE CREATION OF THE DEPARTMENT OF JUSTICE
To spearhead the offensive against the Klan, Grant made an extraordinary and brilliant appointment in June 1870. He named Amos Tappan Akerman of Georgia as the Attorney General of the United States. Akerman was a remarkable figure: born in New Hampshire, he had moved south before the war, married a Southern woman, and reluctantly served as a colonel in the Confederate quartermaster corps out of loyalty to his adopted state. But after Appomattox, Akerman experienced a profound moral conversion. He joined the Republican Party, championed Black voting rights, and publicly declared that the South's only hope lay in strict obedience to federal law and equal protection for all citizens.

Akerman was the first Attorney General to lead the newly created United States Department of Justice, established by Congress in 1870 to centralize all federal law enforcement under a single executive agency. Akerman was a man of incorruptible integrity, fiery energy, and immense moral courage. Operating out of a small, cramped suite of offices in Washington, he personally reviewed thousands of affidavits, witness testimonies, and coroner's reports detailing Klan outrages. He corresponded directly with local district attorneys, military commanders, and terrified victims across the Carolinas, Georgia, and Mississippi. Akerman urged Grant to bypass timid state courts and use the full constitutional authority of the federal government to crush the terrorists before they tore the nation apart again. For Akerman, the struggle was nothing less than finishing the sacred work of emancipation that the Union army had begun.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: THE KU KLUX KLAN ACT OF 1871
In March 1871, President Grant sent an urgent special message to Capitol Hill. 'A condition of affairs now exists in some States of the Union rendering life and property insecure and the carrying of the mails and the collection of the revenue dangerous,' Grant wrote. 'That the power to correct these evils is beyond the control of State authorities I do not doubt; that the power of the Executive of the United States, acting within the limits of existing laws, is sufficient for present emergencies is not clear. Therefore, I urgently recommend such legislation as in the judgment of Congress shall effectually secure life, liberty, and property.'

Congress responded by passing the Third Enforcement Act, commonly known as the Ku Klux Klan Act of 1871. The statute was one of the most revolutionary expansions of federal power in American history. It made state-level civil rights violations and conspiracies to deprive citizens of their constitutional rights federal crimes, punishable in federal courts. It authorized the President to use the United States Army and Navy to suppress domestic violence, and—most drastically—it granted the President the peacetime power to suspend the writ of habeas corpus in areas where armed conspiracies defied the law. When Grant signed the bill into law on April 20, 1871, he was armed with the legal authority to wage total war on domestic terrorism.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: MARTIAL LAW IN THE SOUTH CAROLINA UPCOUNTRY
The ultimate test of Grant's resolve came in the Upcountry of South Carolina, where the Klan had established an absolute reign of terror. In Spartanburg, York, and Union counties, armed bands of hundreds of Klansmen rode openly in broad daylight, murdering Black leaders, breaking into jails to lynch federal prisoners, and forcing thousands of Black citizens to flee their homes and sleep in freezing swamps and pine forests for safety. Entire communities were abandoned as families hid in the woods night after night to escape the torches of the night-riders. Attorney General Akerman traveled personally to Yorkville to investigate the situation firsthand, interviewing terrified refugees and examining whipped and burned victims. He reported back to Grant that the civil authorities were completely terrorized and that only overwhelming federal military force could restore order.

Grant issued a stern proclamation giving the South Carolina Klansmen five days to surrender their weapons and disband. When they defiantly refused, Grant unleashed the hammer. In October 1871, President Grant suspended the writ of habeas corpus across nine counties of South Carolina. He dispatched federal troops, including battalions of the elite 7th Cavalry commanded by Major Lewis Merrill, accompanied by federal marshals and secret service agents. Federal troops swept through the countryside, raiding Klan dens, confiscating arsenals of weapons and disguise robes, and arresting suspects by the hundreds without bail. Terrorists who had bragged of their untouchability and paraded through town squares were suddenly hauled out of bed in the dead of night by federal soldiers bearing fixed bayonets. Within weeks, the military stockades in Yorkville and Columbia were overflowing with hooded vigilantes.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: MASS TRIALS AND THE FALL OF THE INVISIBLE EMPIRE
The federal offensive did not stop with arrests. Akerman and Merrill understood that local white juries would never convict fellow Klansmen in state courts. Therefore, federal prosecutors impaneled interracial juries in federal courts in Columbia, South Carolina, consisting of both loyal white citizens and newly enfranchised Black men—a sight never before seen in Southern history. Federal judges Hugh Lennox Bond and George S. Bryan presided over landmark trials where hundreds of victims took the witness stand to testify courageously against their masked tormentors.

The results were catastrophic for the Invisible Empire. Facing the prospect of long prison sentences in federal penitentiaries in Albany, New York, hundreds of low-level Klansmen broke their solemn blood oaths and turned state's evidence, naming their leaders and detailing the conspiracy's inner workings. Over three thousand Klansmen were indicted across the South; hundreds were convicted or pled guilty, and thousands more panicked and fled the state, seeking refuge in Texas, Arkansas, or the western territories. Nathan Bedford Forrest, terrified of federal arrest, issued a secret order officially disbanding the Ku Klux Klan and commanding all dens to burn their robes and records. By the presidential election of 1872, the first Ku Klux Klan had been completely wiped out of existence. African Americans voted in record numbers that fall, peacefully re-electing Ulysses S. Grant in an overwhelming landslide.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE UNFINISHED REVOLUTION
Ulysses S. Grant's destruction of the first Ku Klux Klan was a monumental victory for civil rights, demonstrating that the federal government possessed both the legal power and the moral will to protect its most vulnerable citizens. Yet the victory carried a tragic postscript. In the mid-1870s, a severe economic depression known as the Panic of 1873 shifted Northern attention away from Southern civil rights. Northern voters grew weary of military interventions, and conservative legal backlash struck at the heart of federal authority. In 1876, the Supreme Court issued disastrous rulings in United States v. Cruikshank and United States v. Reese, gutting key provisions of the Enforcement Acts and stripping the federal government of power to prosecute private racial violence.

Furthermore, Southern white supremacists adapted their tactics, replacing the hooded night-riders of the Klan with open, unmasked rifle clubs and Red Shirts that operated as paramilitary wings of the Democratic Party during the violent election of 1876. Following the disputed Hayes-Tilden election, federal troops were withdrawn from Southern statehouses, ushering in the dark era of Jim Crow disenfranchisement. Yet Grant's precedent was never lost. The Enforcement Acts he championed and enforced lay dormant for eighty years until they were resurrected by the Department of Justice during the 1960s Civil Rights Movement to prosecute the murderers of civil rights workers in Mississippi and Alabama. In an age of terror, Ulysses S. Grant had proven that the American Republic could defend the freedom of all its people.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
Ulysses S. Grant's decisive war against the Ku Klux Klan demonstrated an unwavering commitment to the promise of equal citizenship forged in the crucible of the Civil War. Though the shadows of Jim Crow would soon descend upon the South, the legal framework and moral courage Grant established laid the groundwork for the modern civil rights era. Next week, we move forward to the Gilded Age with Rutherford B. Hayes and the disputed election of 1876 that brought Reconstruction to its bitter conclusion. Until then, thank you for listening to Most Fascinating Stories.
